levels.title: First Steps
levels.blurb: Meet rules, selectors, colors, and your first text styles.

levels.title: Boxes & Units
levels.blurb: Learn how every element is a box and how CSS measures it.

levels.title: Cascade Rules
levels.blurb: Discover which rule wins and how to target elements precisely.

levels.blurb: Line things up with flexbox and build simple grid layouts.

questions.prompt: Which rule makes the text of every `<h1>` on the page green?
questions.hint: A rule has a selector, then declarations inside curly braces.
questions.explain: `h1 { color: green; }` is a CSS rule: the selector `h1` picks every `<h1>`, and the declaration sets its text color. `.h1` targets `class="h1"` instead, and the other two are not valid CSS.

questions.prompt: In a CSS rule, the declarations go inside curly braces `{ }`.
questions.hint: Picture the shape of a normal rule.
questions.explain: A rule is a selector followed by a block in curly braces. The declarations, like `color: red;`, live inside that block.

questions.prompt: In this rule, what is `color` called?
questions.hint: It is the thing being changed, not what it is changed to.
questions.explain: In a declaration like `color: red`, `color` is the property and `red` is the value. The selector (`p`) chooses which elements get the style.

questions.prompt: Which character separates one declaration from the next inside a rule?
questions.hint: Look at the end of each line in a typical rule.
questions.explain: Each declaration ends with a semicolon, so the browser knows where one stops and the next begins. The colon is different: it sits between the property and its value.

questions.prompt: How do you write a comment in CSS?
questions.hint: CSS has only one comment style, with an opening marker and a closing marker.
questions.explain: CSS comments start with `/*` and end with `*/`. They can span many lines. `//` is not a comment in CSS.

questions.prompt: What does this rule style?
choices:
Only the first `

` element on the page
questions.hint: There is no dot or hash in front of the name.
questions.explain: A bare element name is a type selector. It matches every element of that type, so this makes all paragraphs gray.

questions.prompt: Which are real ways to add CSS to an HTML page? Select all that apply.
choices: A `<link>` element that points to a `.css` file
questions.hint: One of these elements does not exist in HTML.
questions.explain: You can link an external file, write CSS in a `<style>` element, or use an inline `style` attribute. There is no `<css>` element in HTML.

questions.prompt: Type the property name that chooses the typeface, as in `___: Arial, sans-serif;`.
questions.hint: It has two words joined by a hyphen and starts with `font`.
questions.explain: `font-family` takes a list of fonts. The browser uses the first one it has, so ending with a generic family like `sans-serif` is a good fallback.

questions.prompt: Which selector targets every element with `class="card"`?
questions.hint: Class selectors start with a small punctuation mark.
questions.explain: A class selector starts with a dot, so `.card` matches every element whose class list includes `card`.

questions.prompt: Which selector targets the element with `id="header"`?
questions.hint: Class selectors start with a dot. Id selectors use a different symbol.
questions.explain: An id selector starts with `#`. Note that plain `header` is a type selector that matches `<header>` elements instead.

questions.prompt: The same class name can be used on many elements on the same page.
questions.hint: Think about how a class is different from an id.
questions.explain: Classes are made for reuse. You can put `class="button"` on as many elements as you like, and one `.button` rule styles them all.

questions.prompt:
Which selectors match this element: `

Hi

`? Select all that apply.
questions.hint: The element has a type and a class, but no id.
questions.explain: `p` matches by element type, `.intro` by class, and `p.intro` requires both. `#intro` would need `id="intro"`, which this element does not have.

questions.prompt: Which property changes the color of text?
questions.hint: The name is a single, short word.
questions.explain: The `color` property sets the text color (the foreground color) of an element.

questions.prompt: Which property fills the area behind an element's content with a color?
questions.hint: Think of what sits behind the text.
questions.explain: `background-color` paints the background of the element, including the padding area.

questions.prompt: Which color does the hex code `#ffffff` produce?
questions.hint: `ff` is the highest value for each of red, green, and blue.
questions.explain: Hex colors use two digits each for red, green, and blue. `ff` is the maximum, so all three channels at full strength make white. `#000000` is black.

questions.prompt: Type the property name that adds space outside an element's border.
questions.hint: It is the opposite of padding.
questions.explain: `margin` creates space outside the border, pushing other elements away. `padding` is the space inside the border.

questions.prompt: Which property makes text bigger or smaller?
questions.hint: Text styles often share the same first word.
questions.explain: `font-size` sets the size of the text, for example `font-size: 20px`.

questions.prompt: Which declaration makes text bold?
questions.hint: Boldness is about how "heavy" the letters are.
questions.explain: `font-weight` controls how thick the letters are. `bold` is the same as `700`. `font-style` is for things like `italic`.

questions.prompt: `#fff` is too short to be a valid hex color.
questions.hint: Short forms are common in CSS, like `margin: 0`.
questions.explain: CSS accepts 3-digit hex codes as a short form. Each digit is doubled, so `#fff` is the same as `#ffffff`, which is white.

questions.prompt: What does this rule do?
choices: Makes the text inside the `<h1>` bigger and bolder
Centers the `<h1>` vertically on the page
Centers the text horizontally inside the `<h1>`
Moves the whole `<h1>` box to the middle of the screen
questions.hint: The property name begins with `text`.
questions.explain: `text-align: center` centers the inline content, such as text, horizontally inside the element's box. It does not move the box itself.

questions.prompt: Which HTML line loads an external stylesheet called `styles.css`?
questions.hint: The element is usually placed in `<head>` and has a `rel` attribute.
questions.explain: The `<link>` element with `rel="stylesheet"` tells the browser to download and apply a CSS file. The `<style>` element holds CSS written directly in the page, and `<script>` is for JavaScript.

questions.prompt: Which property adds space between an element's content and its border?
questions.hint: Compare it with `margin`. The two properties work on opposite sides of the border.
questions.explain: `padding` is the space inside the border, around the content. `margin` is the space outside the border.

questions.prompt: Which of these are valid ways to write the color red? Select all that apply.
questions.hint: Hex codes can only use the digits 0-9 and the letters a-f.
questions.explain: CSS accepts named colors like `red`, hex codes like `#ff0000`, and functions like `rgb(255, 0, 0)`. Newer CSS also lets you write `rgb(255 0 0)` with spaces instead of commas. `#red` is invalid because `r` is not a hex digit.

questions.prompt: Type the `text-align` value that lines text up against the right edge, as in `text-align: ___;`.
questions.hint: The value names the edge itself.
questions.explain: `text-align: right` lines text up on the right side of its box. In left-to-right languages, `end` gives the same result.

questions.prompt: Which property rounds the corners of a box?
questions.hint: It belongs to the `border` family of properties.
questions.explain: `border-radius` rounds the corners. `border-radius: 50%` on a square makes a circle.

questions.prompt: In this `border` declaration, which part sets the line style?
questions.hint: Other options for this part include `dashed` and `dotted`.
questions.explain: The `border` shorthand combines width (`2px`), style (`solid`), and color (`black`). A border needs a style to show at all.

questions.prompt: Which list shows the parts of the box model from the inside out?
questions.hint: The border sits between the two kinds of spacing.
questions.explain: Every box has content in the middle, then padding, then the border, then margin on the outside.

questions.prompt: What does this `margin` declaration set?
choices: 10px left and right, 20px top and bottom
10px top and bottom, 20px left and right
questions.hint: With two values, CSS pairs opposite sides together.
questions.explain: With two values, the first sets top and bottom, and the second sets left and right.

questions.prompt: This rule changes the width of a `<span>` that has its default display.
questions.hint: Think about which display type ignores width.
questions.explain: Inline elements like a default `<span>` ignore `width` and `height`. Change it to `inline-block` or `block` to size it.

questions.prompt: With the default `box-sizing: content-box`, how wide is this box from border edge to border edge?
questions.hint: Add the padding and border on both the left and right sides.
questions.explain: With `content-box`, `width` is only the content. Add padding (20px × 2) and border (5px × 2): 200 + 40 + 10 = 250px.

questions.prompt: Which `display` values let an element sit in the same line as the text around it? Select all that apply.
questions.hint: Which ones do not force a line break before and after?
questions.explain: `inline` and `inline-block` flow within a line. `block` starts a new line, and `none` removes the element.

questions.prompt: A block element has `width: 300px`. Type the value that centers it horizontally, as in `margin: 0 ___;`.
questions.hint: Let the browser work out the left and right margins.
questions.explain: With `margin: 0 auto`, the browser splits the leftover space equally between the left and right margins. This only works when the block has a width smaller than its parent.

questions.prompt: The `rem` unit is relative to which font size?
choices: The browser window's width and height
The largest font size on the page
questions.hint: The "r" in `rem` is a clue.
questions.explain: `rem` means "root em". `1rem` equals the font size of the root `<html>` element, which is 16px by default in most browsers.

questions.prompt: A length of zero can be written without a unit, as in `margin: 0;`.
questions.hint: Ask yourself whether 0px and 0em could ever be different.
questions.explain: For lengths, `0` needs no unit because 0px, 0em, and 0rem are all the same.

questions.prompt: What does `height: 100vh` mean?
choices: The full height of the parent element
The full height of the viewport
questions.hint: Think about what the letter `v` might stand for.
questions.explain: `1vh` is 1% of the viewport height, so `100vh` is the full visible height of the browser window.

questions.prompt: The parent has `font-size: 20px`. What is the font size of the `<span>` below?
questions.hint: For `font-size`, `em` looks at the parent.
questions.explain: When used in `font-size`, `em` is relative to the parent's font size. So `2em` is 2 × 20px = 40px.

questions.prompt: Which of these are relative length units? Select all that apply.
questions.hint: One of these stays the same no matter what is around it.
questions.explain: `rem`, `em`, and `vh` depend on a font size or the viewport size. `px` is an absolute unit.

questions.prompt: What does `box-sizing: border-box` change?
choices: `width` and `height` include the padding and border
`width` and `height` include padding, border, and margin
The border is drawn inside the padding
questions.hint: It changes what `width` measures.
questions.explain: With `border-box`, the padding and border fit inside the `width` you set. Margin is still added outside. This makes sizes easier to predict, so many projects apply it to every element.

questions.prompt: With `box-sizing: border-box`, how wide is the content area of this box?
questions.hint: The padding and border now come out of the 200px.
questions.explain: With `border-box`, the 200px includes padding and border. The content gets what is left: 200 - 40 - 10 = 150px.

questions.prompt: Type the unit (letters only) where `1` unit equals 1% of the viewport's width.
questions.hint: It is the width partner of `vh`.
questions.explain: `vw` means "viewport width", so `50vw` is half the width of the browser window. `vh` does the same for the height.

questions.prompt: What happens to an element with `display: none`?
choices: It shrinks to the size of its text
It is invisible but still takes up space
It is not shown and takes up no space
questions.hint: Think about whether the layout leaves a gap.
questions.explain: `display: none` removes the element from the layout, so nothing is drawn and no space is kept. Other elements move up to fill the gap.

questions.prompt: `visibility: hidden` hides an element but keeps its space in the layout.
questions.hint: Compare it with `display: none`.
questions.explain: `visibility: hidden` makes the element invisible, but the browser still reserves its space. `display: none` removes it from the layout.

questions.prompt: Which `display` values make an element start on a new line? Select all that apply.
questions.hint: Two of these sit side by side with text, like a word in a sentence.
questions.explain: `block` and `flex` boxes start on a new line and take the full width. `inline` and `inline-block` flow along the line with the text around them.

questions.prompt: What is the default `display` value of a `<div>`?
questions.hint: Think about how two `<div>` elements in a row sit on the page.
questions.explain: A `<div>` is a block element. Block elements start on a new line and fill the available width by default.

questions.prompt: What is the default `display` value of a `<span>`?
questions.hint: Wrap one word of a paragraph in a `<span>`. Does the paragraph break?
questions.explain: A `<span>` is inline. It flows with the text around it and does not start a new line.

questions.prompt: How is `inline-block` different from `inline`?
choices: It accepts `width` and `height` but stays in the line
It stays in the line but ignores `width` and `height`
It always starts on a new line, like a block
It removes the element's padding and margin
questions.hint: It mixes features of inline and block.
questions.explain: An `inline-block` element flows in the line like text, but you can give it a `width` and `height`, like a block. A plain `inline` element ignores `width` and `height`.

questions.prompt: An element has `width: 50%`. What is the 50% measured against?
choices: The height of its parent element
The width of its containing block
The width of the whole browser window
The width of the element's own content
questions.hint: Percentages need something to be a percentage of.
questions.explain: A percentage `width` is relative to the width of the containing block, which is usually the parent element's content box. It is not the whole window, unless the parent is that wide.

questions.prompt: Type the `overflow` value that cuts off any content that does not fit inside the box, as in `overflow: ___;`.
questions.hint: The extra content is not shown at all.
questions.explain: `overflow: hidden` clips content at the padding edge, so anything outside the box is not visible. The default, `visible`, lets content spill out.

questions.prompt: What color are paragraphs with these two rules?
questions.code:
p { color: red; }
p { color: blue; }
questions.hint: The selectors are identical, so look at the order.
questions.explain: When two rules have the same specificity, the one that comes later wins. Here that is `color: blue`.

questions.prompt: These three rules all target the same `<h2 id="main" class="title">`. Which color wins?
questions.hint: Compare ids, classes, and element types.
questions.explain: An id selector is more specific than a class selector, which is more specific than a type selector. So `#main` wins.

questions.prompt: The universal selector `*` is more specific than a type selector like `p`.
questions.hint: Does `*` say anything specific about the element?
questions.explain: `*` has a specificity of (0, 0, 0), so even a single type selector like `p` beats it.

questions.prompt: A link sits inside `<nav class="nav">`. What color is it?
questions.code:
.nav a { color: red; }
a { color: blue; }
questions.hint: Count the classes in each selector.
questions.explain: `.nav a` has one class and one type, which beats `a` with only one type. Specificity matters more than order here.

questions.prompt: What is the specificity of `#nav .item a`, written as (ids, classes, types)?
questions.hint: Count each kind of selector once.
questions.explain: `#nav` is one id, `.item` is one class, and `a` is one type. That gives (1, 1, 1).

questions.prompt: What color is this text?
questions.hint: One of these styles is written directly on the element.
questions.explain: Inline styles in a `style` attribute beat any selector in a stylesheet, including id selectors (unless `!important` is involved).

questions.prompt: Which selectors have the same specificity as `.menu`? Select all that apply.
questions.hint: Think about which column of the specificity count each one adds to.
questions.explain: Classes, attribute selectors, and pseudo-classes all count as (0, 1, 0). An id like `#menu` is (1, 0, 0), which is higher.

questions.prompt: Type the specificity of `nav .link:hover` as three numbers separated by commas, in the order ids, classes, types. For example, `p` is `0,0,1`.
questions.hint: Pseudo-classes go in the same column as classes.
questions.explain: There are no ids. `.link` and `:hover` add two to the class column, and `nav` adds one type. That gives `0,2,1`.

questions.prompt: What does the comma do in this selector?
choices: It applies the rule to both `<h1>` and `<h2>` elements
It matches only elements that are both `<h1>` and `<h2>`
It matches an `<h2>` right after an `<h1>`
questions.hint: It is a way to save writing the same rule twice.
questions.explain: A comma makes a selector list. The rule applies to every element that matches any of the selectors.

questions.prompt: What does the selector `ul li` match?
choices: Only `<li>` elements that are direct children of a `<ul>`
A `<ul>` and every `<li>` on the page
Every `<li>` inside a `<ul>`, at any depth
questions.hint: The space is the descendant combinator.
questions.explain: A space means "descendant". `ul li` matches any `<li>` nested inside a `<ul>`, no matter how deep.

questions.prompt: Which selector matches only `<input>` elements with `type="email"`?
questions.hint: Square brackets check an attribute.
questions.explain: Attribute selectors use square brackets. `input[type="email"]` matches inputs whose `type` attribute is exactly `email`.

questions.prompt: A more specific selector wins over a less specific one, even if it comes earlier in the stylesheet.
questions.hint: Think about what the browser compares first.
questions.explain: The browser compares specificity first. Source order only decides the winner when specificity is equal.

questions.prompt: When does this rule apply?
choices: While the mouse pointer is over the button
After the user has clicked on the button once
questions.hint: Think about what the word "hover" means in plain English.
questions.explain: `:hover` applies while the user's pointer is over the element. It is great for showing that something is interactive.

questions.prompt: What does `li:first-child` select?
choices: Only the first `<li>` on the whole page
The first child element inside each `<li>` element
An `<li>` that is the first child of its parent
questions.hint: The pseudo-class describes the `<li>` itself.
questions.explain: `li:first-child` matches an `<li>` when it is the first child of its parent. Each list can have its own match.

questions.prompt: Which of these are pseudo-classes? Select all that apply.
questions.hint: One of these creates new content instead of describing a state or position.
questions.explain: Pseudo-classes use one colon and describe a state or position, like `:hover` or `:first-child`. `::before` uses two colons because it is a pseudo-element.

questions.prompt: Type the single character used as the child combinator, as in `ul _ li`.
questions.hint: It is a symbol from math comparisons.
questions.explain: `>` is the child combinator. `ul > li` matches `<li>` elements whose direct parent is a `<ul>`.

questions.prompt: Which property controls the space between letters?
questions.hint: The name says exactly what it spaces.
questions.explain: `letter-spacing` adds or removes space between characters. `word-spacing` works between words, and `line-height` sets the height of each line.

questions.prompt: The keyword `inherit` makes a property use the same value as the parent element.
questions.hint: The word itself is the clue.
questions.explain: `inherit` tells the property to take its parent's computed value. It works even for properties that do not inherit by default, like `padding`.

questions.prompt: What line height does this paragraph get?
questions.hint: A unitless value multiplies the font size.
questions.explain: A unitless `line-height` is a multiplier of the element's font size: 20px × 1.5 = 30px.

questions.prompt: What does the selector `ul > li` match?
choices: Every `<li>` inside a `<ul>`, at any depth
`<li>` elements that are direct children of a `<ul>`
`<li>` elements that come right after a `<ul>` as siblings
questions.hint: Compare it with the space in `ul li`.
questions.explain: `>` is the child combinator. It matches only `<li>` elements whose parent is a `<ul>`.

questions.prompt: Which selector gives every even table row a striped background?
questions.hint: The pseudo-class takes a keyword or formula in parentheses.
questions.explain: `:nth-child(even)` matches the 2nd, 4th, 6th children, and so on. `:nth-child(2)` matches only the 2nd row, and pseudo-classes use one colon, not two.

questions.prompt: What does adding `!important` to a declaration do?
choices: It makes the rule load before the rest of the stylesheet
It raises the specificity by one id, like adding `#id`
It shows a warning in the console if another rule overrides it
It beats normal declarations, no matter their specificity
questions.hint: It changes who wins the cascade.
questions.explain: An `!important` declaration wins over normal declarations for that property. It does not change specificity. Instead, it puts the declaration in a stronger group. Use it rarely, because it makes styles hard to override later.

questions.prompt: Which properties are inherited by child elements by default? Select all that apply.
questions.hint: Text-related properties usually pass down.
questions.explain: Most text properties, like `font-family`, `color`, and `line-height`, are inherited. Box properties like `border`, `margin`, and `padding` are not.

questions.prompt: Type the pseudo-class, including its colon, that applies while an element (like an input) is ready for typing, for example after you click into it or reach it with Tab.
questions.hint: It is the word for where your attention is.
questions.explain: `:focus` applies to the element that has keyboard focus. Styling it, as in `input:focus { outline: 2px solid teal; }`, helps users see where they are.

questions.prompt: Which declaration turns an element into a flex container?
questions.hint: Flexbox is turned on with the same property that sets block and inline.
questions.explain: `display: flex` makes the element a flex container, and its direct children become flex items.

questions.prompt: What is the default `flex-direction` of a flex container?
questions.hint: Picture flex items with no extra settings.
questions.explain: The default is `row`, so items are placed left to right in a horizontal line (in left-to-right languages).

questions.prompt: `justify-content` is set on the flex container, not on the flex items.
questions.hint: It arranges all the items together.
questions.explain: `justify-content` describes how the container distributes its items. Properties like `flex-grow` and `align-self` go on the items.

questions.prompt: What does `flex-wrap: wrap` do?
choices: Shrinks every item so they all fit on one line
Stacks all items in a single column
Hides any items that do not fit
Lets items move onto a new line when needed
questions.hint: Think about text wrapping at the end of a line.
questions.explain: By default, flex items stay on one line and shrink if needed. `flex-wrap: wrap` lets them flow onto additional lines instead.

questions.prompt: In a flex container, `align-items` aligns items along which axis?
questions.hint: It is the partner of `justify-content`, which uses the other axis.
questions.explain: `align-items` works on the cross axis, which is perpendicular to the main axis. With `flex-direction: row`, that is vertical.

questions.prompt: What does `flex-direction: column` change?
choices: Each item becomes a table column
Items are placed in a grid of columns
Items stack from top to bottom
Items are placed side by side
questions.hint: The main axis follows the direction you set.
questions.explain: With `column`, the main axis runs top to bottom. Now `justify-content` works vertically and `align-items` works horizontally.

questions.prompt: Which of these are valid `justify-content` values? Select all that apply.
questions.hint: One of these sounds right but is not a CSS keyword.
questions.explain: `center`, `space-between`, and `flex-start` are valid. There is no `middle` keyword; use `center`.

questions.prompt: Type the `flex-direction` value that places items in a row, but in the opposite order (right to left in English pages).
questions.hint: It is the default value with one extra word.
questions.explain: `flex-direction: row-reverse` keeps items in a row but starts from the other end. `column-reverse` does the same for a column.

questions.prompt: In a flex container, `justify-content` aligns items along which axis?
questions.hint: Think about which axis `flex-direction` sets.
questions.explain: `justify-content` works on the main axis, which follows `flex-direction`. With the default `row`, that is horizontal.

questions.prompt: What does `justify-content: space-between` do?
choices: Extra space only after the last item
All items grouped together in the center
Equal space between items, none at the outer edges
Equal space around every item, including the edges
questions.hint: Picture the outer items touching the container's edges.
questions.explain: `space-between` pushes the first item to the start and the last item to the end, then spreads the remaining space evenly between the items. Space around the edges is what `space-around` and `space-evenly` add.

questions.prompt: The `gap` property works in both flexbox and grid layouts.
questions.hint: Is space between items only a problem in grids?
questions.explain: `gap` sets the space between items in both flex and grid containers, and all modern browsers support it in both.

questions.prompt: The container below has one child and a fixed height. Where does the child end up?
choices: In the center, both horizontally and vertically
Centered horizontally, but still at the top
Centered vertically, but still at the left edge
questions.hint: One property handles each axis.
questions.explain: With the default `row` direction, `justify-content: center` centers on the horizontal main axis and `align-items: center` centers on the vertical cross axis.

questions.prompt: What does `gap: 16px` do in a flex container?
choices: Adds 16px of padding inside the container
Adds 16px of space between the items
Adds 16px of margin around each item
questions.hint: Picture two items side by side. Where would the 16px go?
questions.explain: `gap` adds space between items only. There is no extra space before the first item or after the last one.

questions.prompt: Three flex items are each given `flex: 1`. How do they share the container's width?
choices: They keep their content width and stay left
The first item takes all the space
questions.hint: Every item asks for the same share.
questions.explain: `flex: 1` lets each item grow with the same factor, so they split the space equally (as long as their content fits).

questions.prompt: Which properties are set on flex items (the children) instead of the container? Select all that apply.
questions.hint: One of these controls how the whole container breaks lines.
questions.explain: `flex-grow`, `order`, and `align-self` belong on items. `flex-wrap` goes on the container because it decides whether lines wrap.

questions.prompt: A flex container is 600px wide. It has three items, each `width: 100px`, and `gap: 20px`. How many pixels of free space are left? Type a number only.
questions.hint: Count how many gaps sit between three items.
questions.explain: The items use 3 × 100 = 300px. Three items have two gaps, so the gaps use 40px. That leaves 600 - 300 - 40 = 260px.

questions.prompt: What does this create?
choices: A grid with one column and three items
One column that is three times wider
questions.hint: `fr` units share the space.
questions.explain: Each `1fr` gets an equal share of the available space, so this makes three equal columns.

questions.prompt: With `display: grid` and no `grid-template-columns`, items are placed in three columns by default.
questions.hint: Without column tracks, how many columns are there?
questions.explain: Without `grid-template-columns`, the grid has a single column, so items stack in rows. You define columns to place items side by side.

questions.prompt: Which value is the same as `repeat(4, 1fr)`?
questions.hint: `repeat()` writes the pattern out for you.
questions.explain: `repeat(4, 1fr)` repeats `1fr` four times, giving four equal columns.

questions.prompt: How do these two columns share the width of the grid?
choices: The second column is twice as wide as the first
The first column is twice as wide as the second
Both columns are the same width
The second column is 2px wider than the first
questions.hint: Each `fr` is one share of the free space.
questions.explain: `fr` means "fraction". The free space is cut into 3 equal shares: the first column gets 1 share and the second gets 2, so the second is twice as wide.

questions.prompt: The grid container below is 800px wide with no gap. How wide is the second column?
questions.hint: The `fr` column gets what is left after the fixed one.
questions.explain: The first column takes 200px. The `1fr` column gets the remaining free space: 800 - 200 = 600px.

questions.prompt: A grid has three equal columns. What does this rule do to `.wide`?
choices: It spans the first two columns
It sits in column 1 and column 3, skipping column 2
questions.hint: The numbers are grid lines, not columns.
questions.explain: Grid lines are numbered from 1. Going from line 1 to line 3 covers two columns.

questions.prompt: Which of these are valid column sizes inside `grid-template-columns`? Select all that apply.
questions.hint: A track size says how wide a column is.
questions.explain: `1fr`, `200px`, and `auto` all size a column. `span 2` is not a size: it belongs in `grid-column` on an item, to make it cover two columns.

questions.prompt: This grid container is 420px wide. Type the width of each column in pixels (number only).
questions.hint: Take the gap away first, then share what is left.
questions.explain: The gap uses 20px, which leaves 400px of free space. Two `1fr` columns share it equally, so each column is 200px.

questions.prompt: What does `position: fixed` do to this button?
choices: It locks the button's width and height
It stays in the same spot on screen while you scroll
It is placed relative to its parent element
It sits at the bottom of the page, after all the content
questions.hint: Think of a header that is always visible at the top of the screen.
questions.explain: A fixed element is positioned relative to the viewport. It stays in the same spot on screen while the page scrolls, which is why chat buttons use it.

questions.prompt: What does this rule do?
choices: Moves it 10px up, and its old space closes
Moves it 10px down, and its old space stays empty
Moves it to 10px from the top of the page
Moves it 10px down, and nearby elements shift too
questions.hint: The element is shifted from its normal spot.
questions.explain: A relatively positioned element is offset from its normal position. Its original space stays reserved, so nearby elements do not move.

questions.prompt: Setting `top: 20px` on an element with the default `position: static` moves it 20px down.
questions.hint: Think about why many examples add `position: relative` first.
questions.explain: Offset properties like `top` and `left` do nothing on a static element. Give it `position: relative` (or another value that is not `static`) first.

questions.prompt: An element with `position: absolute` is placed relative to what?
choices: Always the top-left corner of the browser window
questions.hint: A "positioned" element has a `position` value other than `static`.
questions.explain: An absolute element uses its nearest ancestor with a `position` other than `static`. If there is none, it uses the initial containing block. That is why parents often get `position: relative`.

questions.prompt: How does this header behave when the page scrolls?
choices: It stays fixed at the top from the very start
It scrolls normally, then sticks once it reaches the top
It is removed from the flow and placed at the top
It scrolls normally and never sticks, because `top` is 0
questions.hint: It acts like two other position values at different times.
questions.explain: A sticky element acts like `relative` until scrolling would push it past the `top` offset. Then it sticks, but only while its containing block is still on screen.

questions.prompt: Elements `.a` and `.b` are siblings that overlap. Which one appears on top?
choices: The one that comes first in the HTML
questions.hint: Think of `z-index` as a stack of layers.
questions.explain: Within the same stacking context, a higher `z-index` is painted in front. So the element with `z-index: 5` is on top.

questions.prompt: Which of these are pseudo-elements? Select all that apply.
questions.hint: Pseudo-elements style a part of an element or add new content.
questions.explain: `::before`, `::after`, and `::placeholder` style parts of an element or generated content. `:hover` is a pseudo-class that describes a state.

questions.prompt: Type the `transform` function name (no parentheses) that makes an element bigger or smaller, as in `transform: ___(1.2);`.
questions.hint: Think of making a map larger or smaller.
questions.explain: `transform: scale(1.2)` draws the element 20% bigger without changing the layout around it. It pairs well with a `transition` for hover effects.

questions.prompt: How do you declare a custom property named `main-color`?
questions.hint: Custom properties start with two of the same character.
questions.explain: Custom properties (also called CSS variables) start with two dashes, like `--main-color`. They are often declared on `:root` so the whole page can use them.

questions.prompt: How do you use the value of a custom property named `--main-color`?
questions.hint: You need a function to read it.
questions.explain: The `var()` function reads a custom property. Writing `--main-color` alone as a value does not look it up.

questions.prompt: Custom property names are case-sensitive, so `--Color` and `--color` are two different properties.
questions.hint: Custom properties are names you invent, not built-in keywords.
questions.explain: Built-in property names are case-insensitive, but custom property names are case-sensitive. `--Color` and `--color` hold separate values.

questions.prompt: What margin does the paragraph inside `.card` get?
questions.hint: Custom properties inherit, and the nearest value wins.
questions.explain:
Custom properties inherit like `color` does. The `

` is inside `.card`, which sets `--gap: 16px`, so that value overrides the one from `:root`.

questions.prompt: If `--accent` is not defined anywhere, what color does this text get?
questions.hint: The second value inside `var()` has a special job.
questions.explain: The second argument of `var()` is a fallback. It is used when the custom property is not defined.

questions.prompt: What does this rule do when the button is hovered?
choices: The background color changes after a 0.3-second delay, with no animation
The button fades out over 0.3 seconds
The background color changes smoothly over 0.3 seconds
questions.hint: A transition animates between two values.
questions.explain: A `transition` animates a property from its old value to its new value. Here, `background-color` changes smoothly over 0.3s when the hover rule applies.

questions.prompt: Which of these are valid media queries? Select all that apply.
questions.hint: Media features describe the device or user settings, not element styles.
questions.explain: Width, orientation, and `prefers-reduced-motion` are real media features. `font-size` is a CSS property, not a media feature.

questions.prompt: Type the `object-fit` value that makes an image fill its whole box, cropping the edges so the image keeps its shape.
questions.hint: It is the opposite of `contain`, which shows the whole image.
questions.explain: `object-fit: cover` scales the image until it covers the box, then crops the extra parts. `contain` shows the whole image, which can leave empty space.

questions.prompt: When does the `.nav` rule in this media query apply?
choices: When the viewport is at least 768px wide
Only when the screen is exactly 768px wide
When the viewport is at most 768px wide
questions.hint: Think about what "min" means in other places, like a minimum age.
questions.explain: A `min-width` media query applies at that width and above. This is the common "mobile first" pattern: start small, then add styles for larger screens.

questions.prompt: What does this rule do?
choices: It stops images from growing wider than their container
It stretches every image to fill the full container width
It crops images to a square
questions.hint: `max` sets an upper limit, not an exact size.
questions.explain: `max-width: 100%` lets an image keep its natural size but never overflow its container. Small images are not stretched, because `max-width` is only an upper limit.

questions.prompt: `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` applies styles when the user's system is set to a dark theme.
questions.hint: The media feature name describes a user preference.
questions.explain: `prefers-color-scheme` reflects the user's light or dark theme setting. It lets you offer a dark design automatically.

questions.prompt: This box is 320px wide. How tall is it?
questions.hint: The ratio is written as width / height.
questions.explain: `aspect-ratio: 16 / 9` keeps the width and height in that ratio. The height is 320 ÷ 16 × 9 = 180px. This is a common size for video players.

questions.prompt: A `::after` rule sets a color and size, but nothing shows up. Which property is most likely missing?
questions.hint: A pseudo-element needs something to show, even an empty string.
questions.explain: `::before` and `::after` are only generated when `content` is set. `content: ""` is enough for a purely decorative shape.

questions.prompt:
Where does this star appear for `

Title

`?
choices: Above the `<h2>`, on its own new line
Outside the `<h2>`, just before its opening tag
questions.hint: Pseudo-elements are generated inside the element.
questions.explain: `::before` creates a generated box as the first child of the element, so the star appears inside the `<h2>`, before its content.

questions.prompt: Which `position` values take an element out of the normal flow? Select all that apply.
questions.hint: Which ones leave no gap where the element used to be?
questions.explain: `absolute` and `fixed` remove the element from the normal flow. `relative` keeps its space, and `static` is the normal default.

questions.prompt: Type the property name that animates a change from one value to another over time, as in `___: color 0.2s;`.
questions.hint: It describes moving smoothly from one state to another.
questions.explain: `transition` animates a property when its value changes, for example on `:hover`. You list the property, then the duration, and optionally a timing function.
